query: How does CoreWeave define and recognize revenue backlog

output.content:
CoreWeave defines **revenue backlog** as (1) remaining performance obligations (“RPO”)—the transaction price allocated to services that are wholly or partly undelivered—**plus** (2) other amounts it estimates will be recognized as future revenue under committed customer contracts; both components remain subject to satisfying delivery and service-availability requirements. [[1]] 

That means backlog is a forward-looking commercial measure, not revenue already earned, invoiced, or necessarily cash collected; it can fluctuate with the timing and size of committed contracts and with the company’s ability to deliver capacity and make services available. [[1]] 

CoreWeave’s committed contracts generally provide cloud-computing capacity for an initial term of one to six years and are typically **take-or-pay**, meaning customers must pay irrespective of utilization. [[2]] CoreWeave recognizes revenue from those arrangements **ratably over the contract period**, rather than recognizing the full contracted value when the agreement is signed. [[2]] 

Customer prepayments are initially recorded as **deferred revenue** and are recognized as revenue as the contracted services are provided under the agreement. [[2]] In contrast, its on-demand arrangements are billed monthly in arrears based on hourly usage. [[2]] 

For scale, at December 31, 2025, CoreWeave reported $66.8 billion of revenue backlog, including $60.7 billion of unsatisfied RPO; management indicated roughly 40% of backlog was expected to be recognized during the following 24 months and roughly 80% during the following 48 months, subject to the delivery and availability conditions. [[1]]
